subject: chemistry

items.q: In chemistry, which of these samples counts as a pure substance?
items.correct: Distilled water, a single compound with nothing else in it
items.misconception: Spring water sold as natural, with nothing added to it
items.why: The everyday sense of pure carries the idea of being in its natural state, and marketing reinforces the link between natural and pure. Origin does not decide purity. Ask only whether the sample is a single element or compound. Many manufactured substances are pure and many natural ones are mixtures.
items.random_wrong: Sea water, because water and salt are both pure chemicals

items.q: A student says a compound cannot be pure because it contains more than one element. What is wrong with this?
items.correct: A compound is one substance, so a compound alone is pure
items.misconception: Nothing is wrong, since only elements can be classed as pure
items.why: Students hear 'more than one kind of atom' and map it onto 'more than one substance'. The word mixture and the idea of being made of different elements get run together. The elements in a compound are chemically combined into one new substance with its own fixed properties. Water is one compound, so a sample of nothing but water is pure. Purity counts substances, not elements.
items.random_wrong: A compound is pure only if just two elements are combined

items.q: Four solid samples were heated gently. Which result shows a pure substance?
items.correct: It melted at 80 degrees C, with no change over a range
items.misconception: It melted steadily between 65 and 79 degrees C as it warmed
items.why: Data tables list one melting point for everything students meet, so the idea that a change of state can be spread over several degrees never appears until purity is taught. Watch the thermometer, not just the final value. A pure substance stays at one temperature while it melts; a mixture melts gradually across a range. The range itself is the evidence of a mixture.
items.random_wrong: It melted between 78 and 82 degrees C, close to the true value

items.q: Liquid A boils steadily at 100 degrees C. Liquid B starts boiling at 97 degrees C and the temperature rises to 103 degrees C. What can be concluded?
items.correct: A is a pure substance and B is a mixture
items.misconception: Both are pure, but B was heated too quickly
items.why: Students are taught to blame apparatus for unexpected results, and a Bunsen burner really does heat unevenly, so the explanation feels well trained rather than evasive. A pure liquid stays at its boiling point however hard it is heated, because the extra energy goes into the change of state. A temperature that climbs while the liquid boils means more than one substance is present.
items.random_wrong: B is pure, since it boiled near 100 degrees C

items.q: A carton is labelled 'pure milk'. What does the label mean?
items.correct: Nothing has been added; chemically the milk is a mixture
items.misconception: The milk is a single compound, so it is chemically pure
items.why: The specification's own point is that the two meanings differ. Advertising uses pure to mean unadulterated and natural, and students meet that use thousands of times before they meet the chemical definition once. Ask what is in the sample, not what has been done to it. Chemically pure means a single element or compound and nothing else. Orange juice contains many compounds, so it is a mixture no matter what the carton says.
items.random_wrong: The milk is pure because it is white with nothing in it

items.q: Which of these is the definition of a formulation?
items.correct: A mixture designed as a useful product, in measured quantities
items.misconception: Any mixture of two or more substances, however it was made
items.why: The definition begins with the word mixture, and students stop reading there. The design and measurement half of the definition is treated as description rather than as part of the test. Apply both halves of the definition. A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product, with each chemical present in a measured quantity for a particular purpose. River water fails on design, purpose and measurement.
items.random_wrong: A liquid in which several solids have been fully dissolved

items.q: Which of these is a formulation?
items.correct: Paint, mixed from pigment, binder and solvent in set amounts
items.misconception: Muddy river water, a mixture of soil, water and dissolved salts
items.why: The definition begins with the word mixture, and students stop reading there. The design and measurement half of the definition is treated as description rather than as part of the test. Apply both halves of the definition. A formulation is a mixture that has been designed as a useful product, with each chemical present in a measured quantity for a particular purpose. River water fails on design, purpose and measurement.
items.random_wrong: Copper, a pure metal drawn into wire for electrical wiring

items.q: A product label lists five ingredients, each with a percentage and a stated job such as cleaning, thickening or perfuming. What does this show?
items.correct: It is a formulation, as each measured part has a purpose
items.misconception: It is a compound, because the parts are in fixed amounts
items.why: Fixed ratios are used earlier as the hallmark of a compound. Students carry that rule across without noticing that in a compound the ratio is fixed by the bonding, not chosen by a manufacturer. In a compound the ratio is fixed by chemistry and cannot be changed. In a formulation the ratio is chosen by the designer and could be changed, which would change the product's properties. The components stay chemically separate.
items.random_wrong: It is a pure substance, since every ingredient is listed

items.q: Why is brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, described as a formulation?
items.correct: Its metals are mixed in measured amounts for useful properties
items.misconception: It is not one, because formulations must be liquid products
items.why: The examples students meet first are usually liquids, and the word formulation sounds like formula, recipe and solution, all of which suggest something poured and stirred. State of matter is irrelevant. What matters is that the product is a designed mixture with measured components. Brass, a fertiliser blend and a loaf of bread all qualify.
items.random_wrong: Its metals combine chemically in a fixed ratio when melted

items.q: In paper chromatography, which statement about the phases is correct?
items.correct: The paper is the stationary phase and the solvent is mobile
items.misconception: The solvent is the stationary phase and the paper is mobile
items.why: Students look at the apparatus at the start, when the solvent is a still pool and the paper is the object being handled, rather than at what moves during the run. Name the phases by what happens during the separation. The solvent travels up the paper, so it is mobile. The paper never moves, so it is stationary.
items.random_wrong: The spots are the stationary phase and the paper is mobile

items.q: Why do the substances in a mixture end up at different heights on a chromatogram?
items.correct: They are distributed differently between the two phases
items.misconception: The lightest particles are carried furthest up the paper
items.why: Separation techniques met earlier, such as filtration and settling, do sort by particle size or density, and gravity offers an intuitive story that fits. The solvent does not lift particles by weight. A substance moves far because it spends more time dissolved in the mobile phase and less held by the paper.
items.random_wrong: Substances held most strongly by the paper travel furthest

items.q: Which substance in a mixture moves furthest up the paper?
items.correct: The one most attracted to the solvent and least to the paper
items.misconception: The one with the smallest and lightest particles in the mixture
items.why: Separation techniques met earlier, such as filtration and settling, do sort by particle size or density, and gravity offers an intuitive story that fits. The solvent does not lift particles by weight. A substance moves far because it spends more time dissolved in the mobile phase and less held by the paper.
items.random_wrong: The one held most strongly by the paper it soaks through

items.q: Which expression gives the Rf value of a substance?
items.correct: distance moved by substance / distance moved by solvent
items.misconception: distance moved by solvent / distance moved by substance
items.why: Students remember that a division is needed but not its direction, and the habit of dividing larger by smaller to avoid decimals decides it for them. Write the equation out before substituting: substance on top, solvent underneath. Because the solvent always travels at least as far as the substance, a correct Rf value can never be greater than 1.
items.random_wrong: distance moved by substance / total length of the paper

items.q: When finding how far a substance has moved on a chromatogram, where is the distance measured?
items.correct: From the pencil line to the centre of the spot
items.misconception: From the pencil line to the top edge of the spot
items.why: Spots spread as they travel, so students look for a single definite boundary, and the leading edge feels like the honest limit of the substance's journey. Use the centre every time. A spot spreads in both directions, so its centre represents the substance's position; using an edge inflates or deflates every Rf value.
items.random_wrong: From the bottom of the paper to the spot's centre

items.q: On a chromatogram the centre of a spot is 3.6 cm from the pencil line, and the solvent front is 8.0 cm from the pencil line. What is the Rf value of the substance?
items.why: Students remember that a division is needed but not its direction, and the habit of dividing larger by smaller to avoid decimals decides it for them. Write the equation out before substituting: substance on top, solvent underneath. Because the solvent always travels at least as far as the substance, a correct Rf value can never be greater than 1.
items.random_wrong: 4.4 cm

items.q: A spot moved 34 mm and the solvent moved 75 mm, both measured to the nearest millimetre. How should the Rf value be given?
items.why: Precision and accuracy are confused: extra digits look like extra care, and there is nothing on the calculator to say where the reliable digits stop. An answer cannot be more precise than the measurements behind it. Distances read to the nearest millimetre give two significant figures, so the Rf value is quoted to two significant figures.

items.q: Why can the same compound have a different Rf value in a different solvent?
items.correct: Its distribution between the phases changes with the solvent
items.misconception: It cannot, because each compound has one fixed Rf value
items.why: Rf is introduced alongside melting point as a way of identifying substances, so students assume it behaves like a constant of the substance alone. Rf describes how a compound is distributed between one particular pair of phases. Change the solvent and the distribution changes, so the value changes. Comparisons are only valid within the same solvent and conditions.
items.random_wrong: In a new solvent the paper always holds the compound more

items.q: A sample gives one spot when run in a single solvent. What can be concluded?
items.correct: It may be pure; it must give one spot in all solvents
items.misconception: It is definitely pure, because only one spot developed
items.why: The rule 'one spot equals one substance' is a fair summary of what is seen and is easy to remember, and students rarely meet a case where two compounds happen not to separate. Two compounds can have the same Rf value in one solvent and travel together as one spot. Repeat the chromatography in a different solvent; only a substance that still gives one spot is evidence of purity.
items.random_wrong: It is the same compound as every sample giving one spot

items.q: Which chromatography result is evidence that a sample is impure?
items.correct: It separated into three spots when one solvent was used
items.misconception: It gave a single spot in each of three different solvents
items.why: The rule 'one spot equals one substance' is a fair summary of what is seen and is easy to remember, and students rarely meet a case where two compounds happen not to separate. Two compounds can have the same Rf value in one solvent and travel together as one spot. Repeat the chromatography in a different solvent; only a substance that still gives one spot is evidence of purity.
items.random_wrong: Its single spot had the same Rf value as a known dye

items.q: In Required practical 6, why is the line on which the spots are placed drawn in pencil?
items.correct: Pencil does not dissolve, so the line stays in place
items.misconception: A pen line works too if the ink is a different colour
items.why: Students know the concern is about confusing the results and think the problem is only one of telling colours apart, rather than of the line itself moving. Ink is itself a mixture of soluble dyes, so it separates and runs, destroying the origin line the measurements depend on. Pencil is insoluble in the solvent and stays where it was drawn.
items.random_wrong: A pencil line can be drawn far more thinly than ink

items.q: In Required practical 6, why must the solvent in the beaker start below the pencil line?
items.correct: Otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent and are lost
items.misconception: Otherwise the solvent cannot dissolve the spots at all
items.why: Dissolving is understood as something that needs immersion, so leaving the spots above the liquid looks as though nothing will happen to them. The solvent rises through the paper by itself and reaches the spots from below. If the spots start below the surface they dissolve straight into the pool of solvent and are lost from the paper.
items.random_wrong: Otherwise the solvent would rise up the paper too fast

items.q: A known dye X has an Rf value of 0.62 in a solvent. A mixture run in the same solvent gives spots at Rf 0.31, 0.62 and 0.85. What follows?
items.correct: The mixture may contain X, along with two other compounds
items.misconception: The mixture is dye X, since one spot has the same Rf value
items.why: The phrase 'used to identify' is read as 'proves the identity of', and students are used to tests that give a definite yes or no answer. The specification says chromatography gives information to help identify substances. Strengthen the evidence by running the unknown and the known side by side in more than one solvent.
items.random_wrong: The mixture cannot contain X, because X gives only one spot

items.q: What can paper chromatography do for a mixture of coloured substances?
items.correct: Separate it and give information helping to identify parts
items.misconception: Name every substance in it without using any known samples
items.why: Textbook chromatograms are drawn with the known substances already labelled, so the labels look as though they came from the paper rather than from separate reference runs. A spot is a position, not a name. Run known substances on the same paper in the same solvent and compare, or compare Rf values obtained under the same conditions.
items.random_wrong: Show how much of each substance the mixture contains

items.q: A colourless, clear liquid with nothing floating in it - is it pure?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Sea water and dilute salt solution both look clear and colourless, and both are mixtures.
items.misconception: If a sample looks clean and clear, with no cloudiness or bits in it, then it is pure.
items.why: Everyday judgements of purity are visual, and filtration in earlier science removes visible solids and leaves a clear liquid, which students read as a purification that has finished the job. Dissolved substances are invisible. Judge purity by evidence about composition, such as a sharp melting or boiling point or a single chromatography spot, not by appearance.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A solid melts between 78 and 82 degrees C, and the data book value is 80 degrees C. Is it pure?
items.correct: No. Melting spread over a four degree range shows a mixture, even though the range happens to straddle the accepted value.
items.misconception: As long as the temperature is close to the book value, the sample is pure; a few degrees either side is just experimental error.
items.why: Students are trained to allow for measurement uncertainty, and they apply that habit to a range that is actually chemical evidence rather than instrument error. Distinguish uncertainty in one reading from a genuine range of melting. A pure solid gives one temperature, read with its own small uncertainty. A sample that keeps melting as the temperature climbs is impure.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an alloy such as brass a formulation?
items.correct: Yes. The specification lists alloys among formulations; the metals are mixed in measured quantities to give the required properties.
items.misconception: Formulations are things made by chemists in the pharmaceutical or paint industry, so medicines and paints count but alloys and foods do not.
items.why: The word formulation is met most often in the context of medicines, and metals are studied in a separate topic, so students file alloys under bonding rather than under mixtures. Learn the specification's own list: fuels, cleaning agents, paints, medicines, alloys, fertilisers and foods. Any designed mixture with measured components counts, whatever industry makes it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A substance is strongly attracted to the paper. Does it travel a long way?
items.correct: No. Being held strongly by the stationary phase keeps a substance near the origin, giving a low Rf value.
items.misconception: The substance that sticks to the paper best must be the one the paper carries furthest, so strong attraction to the paper means a high spot.
items.why: The word attracted is read as helpful rather than as holding back, and students do not picture the paper as a brake acting against the moving solvent. Set the two attractions against each other. Attraction to the paper holds a substance back; attraction to the solvent carries it forward. High Rf means the solvent wins.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are the two distances measured from?
items.correct: Both are measured from the origin, the pencil line: to the centre of the spot, and to the solvent front.
items.misconception: You measure from the bottom edge of the paper, or up to the top of the paper, because those are the ends of the strip.
items.why: The paper's edges are the obvious landmarks and are easy to line a ruler against, while the pencil line looks like a place to put spots rather than a measuring datum. The origin is the starting line for everything. The paper below it and above the solvent front took no part in the separation, so neither edge is measured from or to.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What unit does an Rf value have?
items.correct: None. Rf is a ratio of two distances measured in the same unit, so the units cancel.
items.misconception: Rf comes from measuring lengths in centimetres, so the answer must be in centimetres too.
items.why: Students are correctly drilled to attach units to every measured quantity, and they apply the rule to a derived quantity without checking what happens to the units in the division. Divide the units as well as the numbers: cm divided by cm leaves nothing. Quote Rf as a bare number such as 0.45.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a substance have an Rf value of 1.4?
items.correct: No. The substance is carried by the solvent, so it cannot pass the solvent front; Rf lies between 0 and 1.
items.misconception: In a really good solvent a substance can be pushed past the solvent front, so Rf values above 1 are possible.
items.why: Rf is treated as an abstract number from a formula rather than as a fraction of a journey, so nothing warns the student that a value above 1 is physically impossible. Use the range as a check on your arithmetic. If a calculation gives a number above 1, the two distances have been divided the wrong way round.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Salt is pure and water is pure. Is salt solution pure?
items.correct: No. It contains two compounds, so it is a mixture even though each component on its own is pure.
items.misconception: If every substance you put in was pure, then what you get out must be pure as well, because nothing dirty was added.
items.why: Purity is understood as the absence of contamination, so adding something deliberately and cleanly does not feel like making the sample impure. Purity is about how many substances are present, not how clean they were. One element or compound only is pure; two, however carefully combined, make a mixture.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A solid softens from 70 degrees C and is fully liquid at 80 degrees C. Is it pure?
items.correct: No. It changed state over a ten degree range, so it is a mixture, whatever the final temperature was.
items.misconception: The melting point is the temperature at which melting finishes, so if that final value matches the data book the sample is pure.
items.why: Students watch for the moment the last solid disappears because that is the clearest event to record, and they treat the gradual softening beforehand as warming up. Record the whole range, from the first sign of melting to the last. A pure substance melts entirely at one temperature; a range of any size is evidence of a mixture.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Copper wire is manufactured and useful. Is it a formulation?
items.correct: No. Copper is a pure element, and a formulation must be a mixture.
items.misconception: Anything made deliberately for a job is a formulation, because it was designed as a useful product.
items.why: The memorable part of the definition is 'designed as a useful product', and the requirement that it be a mixture is skipped over as an obvious preliminary. Check for a mixture first. A single element or compound, however useful and however carefully manufactured, cannot be a formulation. Brass is a formulation; pure copper is not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the spots the mobile phase?
items.correct: No. The mobile phase is the solvent; the spots are the substances being separated, carried by it.
items.misconception: The mobile phase must be whatever moves up the paper, and what you watch moving is the coloured spots.
items.why: The colours are the only visible thing that moves, and the solvent front is easy to overlook, so students name the phase after what they can see. The phases are the two things the substances are shared between: the paper and the solvent. The substances being analysed are not a phase at all; they distribute themselves between the two.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does the origin line have to be pencil rather than pen?
items.correct: Because pencil is insoluble in the solvent, so the line does not move or contaminate the chromatogram.
items.misconception: Pencil is used because a sharp pencil draws a thinner, neater line, which makes the distances easier to measure accurately.
items.why: Precision of measurement is a real concern in this practical, so a reason about accuracy sounds sensible and the student never has to think about solubility. The issue is chemical, not geometrical. Ink dissolves in the solvent and runs up the paper with the samples; pencil graphite does not dissolve, so the starting line stays put.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter how deep the solvent is, as long as it touches the paper?
items.correct: Yes. It must be below the origin line, otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent instead of travelling up the paper.
items.misconception: The depth only affects how fast the solvent climbs, so any level that wets the paper will do.
items.why: Students think about the solvent's job of moving up the paper and not about what a pool of solvent would do to a spot sitting in it. Set the level below the pencil line every time. Depth is not about speed; it is about keeping the samples on the paper where they can separate.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a bigger spot mean there is more of that substance?
items.correct: That is not what the specification asks chromatography to show. It separates mixtures and gives information to help identify substances.
items.misconception: The size or darkness of a spot measures how much of the substance the mixture contained, so a chromatogram gives the composition by amount.
items.why: Bigger looks like more in almost every other context, and spot sizes on a real chromatogram do vary noticeably, so the inference is tempting. Read a chromatogram for how many substances are present and how far each has travelled. Use the number of spots and their Rf values, not their size, to answer questions about separation and identity.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.8.1 Purity, formulations and chromatography
